paragraphs.heading: What steel is
paragraphs.text: Steel is iron combined with carbon, and often with other elements too. It has better mechanical properties than pure iron. By definition its carbon content goes up to 2.14%, and plain carbon steels hold between 0.02% and 2.14% carbon by weight. A plain iron–carbon alloy with more than 2.1% carbon is called cast iron instead.

paragraphs.heading: Why carbon makes it strong
paragraphs.text: Carbon slipped into the iron lattice hinders deformation when the metal is under stress, and that is the main source of steel's added strength. The price is paid in ductility: as carbon is added, the metal loses some of pure iron's ability to stretch. Cast iron, with even more carbon, is not malleable even when hot. It is shaped by casting instead, since it melts at a lower temperature than steel and casts well.

paragraphs.heading: Many grades
paragraphs.text: Iron and carbon are always the main ingredients, but other elements produce grades with altered properties. Common additions include manganese, nickel, chromium, molybdenum and vanadium. Stainless steels typically contain 18% chromium and resist corrosion and oxidation better than plain carbon steel. Galvanized steel gets a similar benefit from a coating of zinc. Today the grades are set by various standards organizations.

paragraphs.heading: From pig iron to steel
paragraphs.text: Iron smelted from its ore with coke or charcoal comes out high in carbon and is known as pig iron. To become steel, its carbon must be brought down to the right level, after which other elements may be added. In this refining step, oxygen is injected into the molten iron, where it reacts with carbon to form carbon dioxide gas. In the past, makers tested the cooled metal by trial and error; now chemical analysis can reveal the exact makeup.

paragraphs.heading: A long history
paragraphs.text: Steel was made in bloomery furnaces for thousands of years. Large-scale industrial use began only in the 17th century, with the blast furnace and crucible steel. The Bessemer process, developed in England in the middle of the 19th century, opened an era of mass-produced steel, and mild steel took the place of wrought iron. Later, basic oxygen steelmaking cut costs further and raised quality.

paragraphs.heading: Steel today
paragraphs.text: More than 1.6 billion tons of steel are now made each year, and China produced 54% of the world's supply in 2023. It goes into structures, bridges, ships, trains, cars, tools and appliances. The industry is among the most energy- and emissions-heavy, accounting for 8% of global emissions. On the other hand, steel is one of the most recycled materials, with a global recycling rate above 60%.
